item.title: Aug. 20: Metro Arts Commission Director; a Gun at East High School
item.dc:creator: Banner Staff
item.description:
The interim director of the Metro Arts Commission will get the job full-time after a narrow vote, an East High School brought a stolen handgun to campus, a medical error at Ascension Saint Thomas Midtown resulted in patient injuries and more.

The post Aug. 20: Metro Arts Commission Director; a Gun at East High School appeared first on Nashville Banner.
item.content:encoded:
DIRECTOR’S CHAIR: After a lengthy debate on Wednesday, the Metro Arts Commission voted 5-4 to name interim director Ashley Bachelder to the position permanently. Bachelder has been in the interim role since January 2025. She was brought in from her job at the Metro Human Relations Commission during a period of strife at the commission, which has been working to normalize its grant funding cycles. Some members of the commission preferred a wider search for a permanent director. — Stephen Elliott

STUDENT ARREST: An 11th-grade student at East High School was arrested Wednesday morning after “he attempted to ditch a backpack outside the school with a loaded, stolen handgun inside,” the Metro Nashville Police Department said. The department said a school resource officer initially saw the student carrying two backpacks and later confirmed through surveillance footage that he had left one of them outside the school. Police found a firearm inside that had been reported stolen in March by a woman visiting Nashville from Texas. The gun had been left in her unlocked vehicle overnight. — Steven Hale

DISASTROUS DRUG MISTAKE: At least four people who had joint replacement surgeries at Ascension Saint Thomas Midtown last week suffered serious medical complications after they were mistakenly given potassium instead of the anesthetic bupivacaine, NewsChannel 5 reported Tuesday. The TBI is now investigating, according to a subsequent report. One woman is now paralyzed from the chest down, her family told multiple outlets. The hospital’s president and CEO, Dr. Shubhada Jagasia, acknowledged the incident in a statement and said he was “deeply sorry for the harm caused to our patients.” State officials confirmed to the station that they are investigating. — Steven Hale

PONDERING DATA CENTERS: ThinkTennessee has issued a policy brief that proffers four strategies it believes Tennessee decision-makers should consider to help the state manage the proliferation of data centers. The nonpartisan think tank says large data centers should be treated as grid partners, meaning they should help cover infrastructure costs needed to meet their energy needs; recommends the Tennessee Valley Authority put more of its idle grid capacity to work in order to lower rates for existing customers; invest in transmission infrastructure with an eye toward long-term growth; and allow communities to set their own zoning and permit requirements for data centers. The brief, Powering the Boom, Part II: A Policy Roadmap for Managing Tennessee’s Data Center Growth, notes that more than 1,300 data centers are currently planned across the TVA territory, which includes all or parts of seven states. “By drawing on lessons from other states and regions that are already working through similar pressures, we have a real opportunity to meet the demands for data center growth while still protecting the households and communities that live in the Tennessee Valley,” said Erin Hafkenschiel, president of ThinkTennessee. — David Boclair

OPTIONAL ROUTE: The Tennessee Department of Transportation will partner with DriveTN to add optional toll lanes in each direction of a 26-mile stretch of Interstate 24, between Nashville and Interstate 840 in Rutherford County. The $9.2 billion project is being trumpeted as the country’s largest public-private partnership of its kind and is meant to ease congestion on one of the state’s busiest highways. TDOT will host open house public meetings to discuss the project, from 12:30-6 p.m., Sept. 8 at the Nashville Public Library Pruitt Branch and 12:30-6 p.m., Sept. 9 at the Smyrna Event Center. “We have moved from facing a critical transportation need without a viable path forward to an opportunity that will deliver the project, enhance communities, and improve travel,” TDOT Commissioner Will Reid said in a release. The state projects $24.8 billion in concession value from the choice lanes, and that money can be used to fund future transportation infrastructure projects. Local officials have expressed concern as constituent homeowners and business owners face potential condemnation of their properties to make way for the project. — David Boclair

The post Aug. 20: Metro Arts Commission Director; a Gun at East High School appeared first on Nashville Banner.

item.title: Across Nashville Neighborhoods, Parked Waymos Are Recording You
item.dc:creator: Sarah Grace Taylor
item.description:
Waymo vehicles in Nashville and elsewhere record audio and 360-degree video while parked in various neighborhoods and business districts, raising privacy concerns due to a lack of clear public guidelines regarding data storage and usage.

The post Across Nashville Neighborhoods, Parked Waymos Are Recording You appeared first on Nashville Banner.
item.content:encoded:
Parked Waymo vehicles are recording Nashville neighborhoods, churches, businesses and parks every day without any public guidelines on how long footage is stored, and minimal details on how it is used.

Since the company fully launched in Nashville in June, more than 50 white, driverless Jaguars with out-of-state plates and large, spinning sensors shaped like top hats on their roofs have been carting people around Nashville, saturating downtown hotspots like the riverfront, Lower Broadway and Music Row.

The vehicles use a combination of radar and LiDAR sensors, external audio and video from both the in-car camera system and the 29 external cameras to operate and train the vehicles when they’re underway.

But even when they are vacant, if the vehicles are running — which is identifiable by the sensors spinning and whirring — they are recording audio and 360-degree video to “continuously perceive the world around the vehicle.”

Ethan Teicher, a spokesperson for Waymo, told the Banner last week that the constant recording is necessary for the parked vehicles to respond to, say, emergency vehicles or other hazards when parked, but the vehicles “are engineered with privacy-by-design.”

“The sensors remain active while the vehicle is parked to maintain awareness of its surroundings and move from that location when required,” Teicher continued.

Asked how long the data recorded is stored, the company said it’s too costly to store large amounts of random footage or audio that doesn’t directly help train the vehicles or pertain to a specific incident, involving the Waymo or otherwise.

When asked, the company did not provide any specific policy on when and how idly collected data is used, but rather said retention is determined on a case-by-case basis.

“Waymo retains data for a reasonably appropriate amount of time to improve our automated driving system,” Teicher wrote. 

Waymo would not specify whether it has different policies for recording residential or other potentially sensitive areas, but said the company “only collects and uses the minimum information reasonably appropriate to” improve automated driving.

But between rides, the vehicles are frequently stationed in low-traffic street parking, which the company says helps reduce the impact on traffic as they await trips, recording areas across Nashville.

Where they park

The company wouldn’t say how many designated or frequented parking areas exist in the city, but Nashvillians have noticed several hot spots where the vehicles repeatedly sit idly. In these spots, the vehicles park several times per week, sometimes for prolonged periods, and sometimes more than one vehicle at a time. 

In the last week, the Banner visited 12 street parking spots where Waymos reportedly parked frequently and found vehicles parked in 10 of those on the first visit. 

The vehicles were parked and sensors were visibly running without any occupants in each spot, including residential areas in North Nashville, East Nashville and Wedgewood, near businesses on Spence Lane and in South Nashville.

The spots included some more discreet locations, like behind the Church of Scientology off of Eighth Avenue, and others with lots of people in sight, including high-foot-traffic residential streets overlooking Reservoir Park and behind the Eastland Kroger. 

At Lenore Street and 7th Street, two Waymos were parked about 100 yards apart, both running and presumably recording. On Scovel Street, Waymos have been parking in front of several homes and two churches since June, sometimes for hours at a time. 

Some in Nashville didn’t know the vehicles were recording and expressed concerns about Waymo contributing to the growing number of private companies recording people in public, including a woman named Rachel, who did not agree to share her last name, but lives in an apartment in East Nashville near one of the frequent parking spots. 

“Oh hell no, I don’t like that at all. That thing is parked outside of my house all the time,” Rachel said. “It’s just another of these private companies spying on us.” 

Rachel added that she didn’t like the company having carte blanche to record everything around its vehicles, even without consent, like when a rider has to agree to terms and conditions.

“It feels like the last couple of years has been one company after another monitoring people and we have no real idea what they’re doing with that video,” Rachel continued. 

“And it’s not like they announced that they’re recording us, they’re probably not gonna tell us if they start sharing with another company down the line,” she added. 

Not all neighbors mind their presence, like Jon Martinez, who lives with his fiancé and child in North Nashville, directly across from one of the spots where Waymos park multiple times per week. Martinez described himself as a “big fan” of the company, noting that he and his family prefer taking the autonomous vehicles over riding with a stranger. 

“The most dangerous thing on the roads is definitely the people,” Martinez said, defending the company. “Especially in Nashville.”

Noting that he has multiple Ring cameras and lives in a neighborhood with notable foot traffic and safety concerns, Martinez said he doesn’t mind Waymos contributing to the surveillance ecosystem. 

“Realistically speaking, this street in particular has historically been more of an unsafe street,” said Martinez, who has lived in his home for four years. “Do I love being recorded? No. … Do I think an extra layer of recording is good? Probably.” 

Who has access to the footage?

Private companies doing surveillance and sharing the data they collect has become increasingly prevalent in recent years and has been front of mind in Nashville with plans for license plate readers on state highways and implementation at the airport. At the center of privacy concerns around LPRs is the surveillance company Flock, which aggregates data from its cameras and provides it to users, including law enforcement.

Last week, 404 Media reported that Flock was trying to broker a deal to access in-car footage from rideshare apps Uber and Lyft to add to its sweeping surveillance network. In a nutshell, Flock proposed accessing Nexar dash cameras in 350,000 delivery and rideshare vehicles, but the deal never materialized.

Still, the idea raises questions about how the burgeoning robotaxi company will share data with its partners, which include Lyft, Uber and Nexar.

When asked if Waymo shared its footage with Uber, Lyft, Flock or Nexar, the company acknowledged a “research agreement” between Waymo and Nexar, but insisted that they “do not partner with any organization for the purpose you mentioned.” 

What Waymo shares with law enforcement has been sporadic.

Waymo has repeatedly provided stored footage to law enforcement across the country, but says that the general practice is to only share minimal information to lawful requests, though in a July incident, a self-driving Waymo reported two teenagers for drinking and using toy guns, delivering the riders to San Mateo Police.

In another instance footage requested by San Francisco police in connection to a robbery was not provided, despite a warrant, because the company was no longer storing the footage by the time police requested it, lending credence to the company’s claim that mundane footage is not being stored for extended periods of time. 

“When we receive requests for information from law enforcement, we carefully review each request to ensure it satisfies applicable laws and is legally valid. We will closely scrutinize each request, narrow its scope or push back as needed,” Teicher said, also offering that the company does “not use facial recognition or other biometric identification technologies to identify individuals, and we only retain data necessary for the continued improvement of the Waymo Driver.”

A spokesperson for the Metro Nashville Police Department said they were unaware of any instances in which the department had requested material from Waymo. The Tennessee Highway Patrol did not respond to the same question.

As Waymo gets underway in Nashville, Elon Musk’s Tesla appears to be plotting a local launch of its own untested autonomous vehicle service, after a fleet of 15 gold Tesla Cybercabs were spotted in Franklin last week. Tesla has been repeatedly found in violation of its own privacy policy by recording and storing sensitive and less-than-anonymous footage through its consumer-owned vehicles.

The post Across Nashville Neighborhoods, Parked Waymos Are Recording You appeared first on Nashville Banner.

item.title: Aug. 19: Vanderbilt Provost Gets a New Job; Restore Our Fairgrounds Coalition Rallies Support
item.dc:creator: Banner Staff
item.description:
Vanderbilt University Provost C. Cybele Raver has been named president-designate at the University of Michigan. The Restore Our Fairgrounds Coalition continues its signature drive to amend the Metro Charter regarding the Fairgrounds Nashville speedway.

The post Aug. 19: Vanderbilt Provost Gets a New Job; Restore Our Fairgrounds Coalition Rallies Support appeared first on Nashville Banner.
item.content:encoded:
MOVING ON: C. Cybele Raver, provost and vice chancellor for academic affairs at Vanderbilt University, has been named president-designate at the University of Michigan. The UM board of regents is expected to formally approve her appointment on Sept. 1. She will continue in her current role until Oct. 31 and assume her new office on Dec. 1. “Cybele’s impact on Vanderbilt has been profound,” VU chancellor Daniel Diermeier said in a release. “Her leadership has strengthened the university at every level — advancing our academic ambitions, accelerating discovery and innovation, and creating the conditions for our faculty, students and schools to thrive.” Daniel Reisberg, vice chancellor for operations and the campus network, will chair the search committee, and the university has partnered with a search firm to identify Raver’s replacement. Tiffiny Tung, vice provost for undergraduate education and growth initiatives, Ingram Chair in Anthropology and professor of anthropology and archaeology, will serve as interim provost upon Raver’s departure. — David Boclair

ANOTHER ROUND: With a month remaining in their push to collect signatures and get a charter amendment on the ballot, the Restore Our Fairgrounds Coalition rallied support Tuesday and released images of what a Fairgrounds Nashville without the Fairgrounds Speedway could look like. Members of the group were joined by elected officials Metro Councilmember Terry Vo and state Reps. John Ray Clemmons and Caleb Hemmer, who expressed support for the ballot initiative. If the initiative makes it on the ballot and wins a majority at the polls, it would remove a Metro Charter requirement that auto racing be conducted at the fairgrounds. Clemmons’ and Hemmer’s colleague Rep. Aftyn Behn recently expressed her opposition to the proposal. While reiterating that it was just one idea and that the community could develop others, the group displayed renderings of a pavilion, park and affordable housing building at the site, home to the racetrack for decades. They also displayed a drawing of the facility as it stood before the racetrack was built, when it was a public park, as the coalition seeks to counter racetrack supporters’ argument that the track is a historic facility that needs to be preserved. — Stephen Elliott

The post Aug. 19: Vanderbilt Provost Gets a New Job; Restore Our Fairgrounds Coalition Rallies Support appeared first on Nashville Banner.

item.title: How One Nashville Family Chose Between Public, Charter and Private Schools
item.dc:creator: Lillian Avedian
item.description:
As Nashville families return to school during an era of expanding school choice, the experiences of Camelia Russell and her children highlight both the potential benefits of charter and private alternatives and the financial and systemic barriers that remain for many in Tennessee.

The post How One Nashville Family Chose Between Public, Charter and Private Schools appeared first on Nashville Banner.
item.content:encoded:
“I always tell them, I want y’all to be better than me,” Camelia Russell said of her children, 16-year-old Devine and 15-year-old Amelia. “I don’t want y’all to be living how I am struggling. I want y’all to have futures, careers and, you know, have a good life.”  

Both children attended May Werthan Shayne Elementary and William Henry Oliver Middle, public schools in southeast Nashville. Since then, the path toward those hoped-for futures has been – at times – difficult to navigate.

In May, as Russell watched her daughter finish her first year at a new charter school, she was filled with pride. After switching schools twice in as many years, Amelia finally landed at Nurses Middle College, where she was happy. 

Yet her son Devine was on her mind. Devine had been struggling for two years at John Overton High School. Russell had read about the new voucher program and felt hopeful that she could find a better educational opportunity for her son outside of the public school system. 

Nashville’s families are returning to school this month at a moment of expansion for school choice programs. Davidson County is home to 40 charter schools, which are privately run but publicly funded, with more opening each year. Tennessee is also entering the second year of a statewide voucher program — known as the “Education Freedom Scholarship” — that awarded 35,000 families $7,530 in public funds to pay for private school tuition and fees. In Davidson County 45 private schools are accepting vouchers this year. 

Families are now learning how to seek information about an ever-growing list of schools and navigate complicated education programs. Russell and her children’s story provides a window into why some families opt into school choice programs — as well as the barriers to accessing those choices. 

‘The worst two years of my life’

Devine goes to Bible study every Wednesday. After he was baptized this spring, his 6-foot frame dipped into the water, he stood in the baptism pool and hugged his pastor tightly for a long time. He has played football on the school team for years as an offensive and defensive lineman. His dream is to play for the Tennessee Titans. 

“I’m just trying to make it … for my mom, make it for my dad,” he said. “I’m just trying to make it a better life for them.” 

Camelia described her son like a teddy bear.

“Sweetest thing in the world, but I know it’s a grizzly in there. And you poke the bear enough, they’re going to show themselves,” she said. “My baby is a teddy bear, but these school systems have changed him.”

After middle school, Devine followed his friends to John Overton High, where, for two years, he was bullied by his peers. They picked on his appearance and called him “fat” and “ugly.” One day he was walking up the stairs to the cafeteria for lunch. One of the boys snuck up and tried to pull down his pants. Devine reacted immediately and was ready to fight back. They had “poked the bear,” in his mom’s words. Several people had to intervene.

Devine wrapped his arms around himself while recounting these stories. 

“Those were the worst two years of my life,” he said. “I never knew I could truly be hated by someone. That’s what I felt at Overton. I cried a lot about it, because it hurt.” 

“It’s gonna leave a stain on me, because now I have to remember that for as long as I live,” he continued. 

We want to hear from families about your experience with school choice in Nashville, whether positive or negative. Have you considered applying to the voucher program? What was the application process like for you? How are you navigating public, private and charter school options? If you’d like to share your story, please email lavedian@nashvillepublicmedia.com.

He started to make excuses to skip classes and football practice. He would call his mom from school in the mornings and fabricate headaches and stomach pain. 

“We do not tolerate bullying of any kind, and we take concerns brought to our attention seriously,” Overton Principal Dr. Kelby Garner said in an emailed statement. “We consistently encourage students and families to share concerns with us so they can be addressed promptly and appropriately.”

The district said that schools cannot discuss the specific circumstances of a student due to federal privacy requirements. 

“I fear for my son over there,” Russell said. “My son is 6-foot-1, and he’s 300 pounds. Unfortunately this is the world we live in. Me raising a young Black man that big, he’s intimidating just by his looks and his size.” 

She wept. 

“Why would I send my son back over there?” she continued. “I pray to God that he have a better next school year, wherever he is.” 

‘I want my mom to be proud of me’

When the family moved from Antioch to Hermitage two years ago, Russell’s daughter Amelia was willing to try something new and enrolled at STRIVE Collegiate Academy for her last year of middle school. 

She did not feel welcomed at the charter school. The students were rude, she said, and the staff were not supportive. 

“That school damaged my personality,” she said. “I was broken. I was sad all the time.” 

She gradually turned inward. One week she came home from school crying three days in a row. 

“She was a really happy child. She smiled a lot,” Russell said. “But they sabotaged my baby, the kids did.” 

At a high school fair, they met Dr. Andrea Poynter, executive director of Nurses Middle College, a new charter school opening in southeast Nashville the following fall. Nurses MC prepares students to enter careers in nursing and healthcare directly out of high school. 

Amelia wasn’t sure she wanted to be a nurse. She likes to draw and write music, and had thought of becoming an artist. But she knew she wanted to help people and that nursing could lead to a stable and purposeful career, so she enrolled and joined the school’s first cohort of freshman students. 

“I feel like I’m doing something good,” she said. “I want to make a name for myself. I want my mom to be proud of me.”

The school has faced challenges common at new charter schools. The campus is small, and Amelia said the first week back has felt “cramped” and “chaotic” with the addition of a second freshman class. Also, she has spent upwards of 90 minutes on one of the school’s four buses as it drove across the city. 

Even so, at Nurses MC, Amelia opened up again. She found a good circle of friends and repaired her self-esteem. She passed an exam to enter a Licensed Practical Nursing program in partnership with TCAT Nashville. 

Dr. Poynter said she’s optimistic that the school will find a larger facility. She’s waiting to hear about procuring a fifth school bus. Still, she said that the school has had a relatively smooth opening, because she raised significant funds through grants. Yet she has heard from fellow charter school founders who struggle with these logistics. 

“I didn’t realize until after I opened the school that charter schools are a political hot button here in Nashville,” Poynter said. “Either we’re doing the job that we’re supposed to do for [the kids] or we’re not, and if we’re not, then what are we going to do to fix it?”

‘The only way it can ever work’

Seeing Devine struggling, Russell started the search for a new school for her son. 

She wanted a Christian private school that reflected the family’s faith. She knew she couldn’t afford the tuition, but a friend told her that with the help of a state voucher and scholarships, he paid just a few hundred dollars a month. Russell considered that selling pies and cutting spending elsewhere could make up the cost. 

“If I have to sacrifice a lot of different things, I’ll do that for my son,” she said. 

The voucher program has been the centerpiece of Gov. Bill Lee’s education agenda. After a six-year fight and millions spent by out-of-state pro-voucher groups, the legislature passed the governor’s universal voucher bill in January 2025. This year the legislature voted to grow the program from 20,000 to 35,000 seats, directing about $260 million in public funds to private schools.  

The bill passed by a narrow margin, due to concerns from public school advocates and some Republican legislators from rural areas that school choice programs divert critical funds and resources away from public education.  

“We know that parents know best. Clearly, Tennesseans like freedom,” Gov. Lee said in February. “This is why we should empower parents.”

Russell sat down to complete an online application for one private Christian school that Devine had toured and loved, but when she reached the final page, she stopped: The application required a $100 fee and $500 deposit.

“And I was like, I don’t have it,” she said.

School choice programs promise to create educational opportunities that families otherwise could not access. Yet in the voucher program’s second year, those choices are still limited based on a family’s household income.  

An “Education Freedom Scholarship” is worth $7,530, which is less than the tuitions at most Davidson County private schools that opted into the voucher program, which range from $6,000 to $30,000 a year. That does not include additional expenses including application fees, uniforms, textbooks, field trips and more. Families also need to find appropriate transportation when private schools don’t offer busing. These obstacles are already inhibiting families like Russell’s from participating in the program. 

Most vouchers for the 2026-27 school year went to higher-income families, according to state data. Just 3,970 of about 16,000 families were in the lowest income category. The largest share — 9,360 —  are in the higher income category, families of four that make up to $180,000 a year. 

The Department of Education has not published data on the prior school enrollment of voucher recipients. But some Republican legislators have hinted that the program is largely benefitting families who could already afford private school tuition. Rep. Tim Hicks, a Republican from East Tennessee, said he had seen state data showing that most vouchers went to students already enrolled at private schools.

“That is exactly the only way it can ever work,” he said. “It’ll get filled up, and more and more folks, eventually through the years, will come and start taking advantage of this program.” 

‘The best I’ve ever felt’

Stumped by the steep private school application fee, Russell moved on from the voucher program. 

An ad for a charter school called Nashville Collegiate Prep kept popping up in her Facebook feed. As a selling point, the school was advertising its new football coach Jamie Graham, the former coach at Lipscomb Academy. She reached out, and the school responded the same day. 

Public school advocates in Nashville often lament that they can’t compete with the marketing efforts used by charter schools to recruit families. Dr. Sharada Deaton, the former principal at Wright Middle, previously told the Banner that charter school competition in southeast Nashville has affected enrollment at public schools. 

“This area and Antioch area you see a preponderance of charter schools who have very … novel ways of recruiting parents, right? They attract families to their schools,” she said, adding that “dwindling enrollment also means dwindling budget.” 

Still, charters aren’t necessarily growing across the board. Enrollment at Nashville’s public and charter schools has declined over the last six years. MNPS enrolled 78,222 students in 2025-26, compared to 81,685 students in 2020-21, while charter school enrollment dropped from 13,422 to 12,527 in that period. 

In fact, Devine’s sister Amelia would be one of the last students to attend STRIVE. After 11 years in Nashville, STRIVE closed this year due to low enrollment and the sale of its facilities. Between 2021-22 and 2025-26 enrollment at STRIVE dropped from 337 to 177 students. Meanwhile, school options are multiplying, leaving a growing number of schools to attract a shrinking pool of students. 

On the last day of school, Devine was feeling down. He couldn’t wait to get out of Overton. His mom picked him up and said she had coach Graham on the phone. 

Devine and Graham talked in the car for hours. Graham talked about his upbringing and learning the three Bs: Bible, books and ball. Devine shared his dreams of going to college and playing football. The coach promised that he would help Devine get into college tuition-free. 

“I genuinely feel like I built a bond with him through the phone,” Devine said. “Someone I can really trust as a coach, you know, and as a friend. … He’s just honest and truthful.” 

Devine enrolled at Nashville Collegiate Prep as a junior and attended summer football practices. From the start, he felt a difference. The coach and players made him feel welcomed and accepted, “the best I’ve ever felt in my whole life,” he said.  

Many of his fellow students shared similar stories and had transferred to NCP from nearby public schools.  

‘They love my kids’

Russell feels relieved entering the new school year. She’s met the administration and staff at Nurses MC and Nashville Collegiate Prep and trusts that the students are safe and supported. She appreciates the smaller class sizes and doesn’t worry about whether the students are being supervised or whether an incident in the cafeteria could go unnoticed. 

Picking the right school isn’t just about the quality of education, she said, but rather the safety — physical and emotional — of your children. 

“They love my kids just as much as I love my kids,” she said. “Metro, it wasn’t the same.”

The post How One Nashville Family Chose Between Public, Charter and Private Schools appeared first on Nashville Banner.

item.title: Her Name Was Tasha: Friends Mourn Unhoused Nashvillian Killed While Sleeping Underneath Semi-Truck
item.dc:creator: Steven Hale
item.description:
A 46-year-old woman named Tasha died after she was run over while she slept under a semi-truck trailer at a southeast Nashville Shell station on Monday.

The post Her Name Was Tasha: Friends Mourn Unhoused Nashvillian Killed While Sleeping Underneath Semi-Truck appeared first on Nashville Banner.
item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday morning, a woman named Kay sat on a tree-shaded curb facing a row of semi-trucks parked behind a Shell station in southeast Nashville. Yes, she said, she knew the woman who had died there less than 24 hours earlier. Her name was Tasha. 

The two had been friends for 20 years, Kay said, living on the streets of Murfreesboro and Nashville. More recently, they were part of a small group of unhoused people who often seek refuge in that parking lot among the big rigs and their resting drivers. When Kay got there Monday afternoon, she saw an ambulance. 

“I walked up and she was gone,” she told the Banner.  

The Metro Nashville Police Department said Monday that the 46-year-old woman had been sleeping underneath a semi-truck trailer when its driver pulled out of the parking spot around 2:30 p.m., running her over. They said the driver, who did not stop, “may not have known that the woman was run over.”

MNPD spokesperson Brooke Reese told the Banner on Tuesday that the medical examiner’s office was still working to confirm her identity. 

Kay said Tasha’s boyfriend had been at the scene on Monday, but she wasn’t sure about any other family that she had. She spoke about her friend not as someone she’d been living around but as a person she’d been surviving with. When Kay suffered an accidental overdose last month, she said, Tasha had rushed to her aid. Sitting on the curb next to Kay, Michael Keys said Tasha had always been kind. 

“She was down and out, but a heart of gold,” he said.

Both said it’s common for people to rest in the shade beside or even underneath the parked semi-trucks, usually staying away from the tires. It was above 90 degrees on Monday afternoon when Tasha would have crawled under one. The drivers, Kay said, are “really nice” and often give out water. They are also supposed to inspect outside their vehicles before taking off again. A driver sitting in the cab of his truck nearby confirmed as much. He declined to give his name, as he was on the job, but said if the incident happened the way it’s been described then the driver was in the wrong.  

Keys said he’d fight to make sure people don’t just move on from his friend’s death. 

“I’m not letting this go,” he said. “She’s not going out like that.” 

Kay began to cry as she expressed her doubts about what comes next. 

“I doubt they’re really going to investigate because of what we do — because of where we are,” she said. “It’s just one less problem for them … But we’re still somebody’s mother or sister or daughter.”

The post Her Name Was Tasha: Friends Mourn Unhoused Nashvillian Killed While Sleeping Underneath Semi-Truck appeared first on Nashville Banner.

item.title: Key O’Connell Aide Steps Down From Nashville Mayor’s Office
item.dc:creator: Stephen Elliott
item.description:
Metro's chief of operations and performance Kristin Wilson announced her resignation from the mayor's office. Her final day will be Aug. 28.

The post Key O’Connell Aide Steps Down From Nashville Mayor’s Office appeared first on Nashville Banner.
item.content:encoded:
Metro’s chief of operations and performance Kristin Wilson is out at the mayor’s office after seven years. 

Wilson joined Metro at the start of Mayor John Cooper’s term in 2019 and helped lead the city’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic. She was retained when Mayor Freddie O’Connell took office in 2023. 

Her responsibilities have included overseeing Metro department leaders. Wilson previously was deputy chief operating officer for Atlanta and worked at a Nashville insurance company. 

She resigned on Monday, according to the mayor’s office. Her last day will be Aug. 28.

In a resignation letter, Wilson wrote that she was grateful to Cooper and O’Connell and said it is time “to take a pause, to reflect on the work accomplished and my priorities for my career and life path going forward.”

“Though the work is not done, and as a city is always responding to changing needs of its constituents and many macroeconomic and existential contexts it does not control, it may never be fully complete,” Wilson wrote. “But I do leave Metro believing it’s in a better operational place than it was when I started; that the leaders and employees of Metro have felt led, supported, challenged and recognized in ways I have directly contributed; and that the foundation for them to meet challenges and opportunities ahead is as strong as it has ever been.” 

O’Connell has one year remaining in his term and publicly launched a reelection campaign this summer. 

“I’m grateful to Kristin for her service to Metro over the last seven years,” O’Connell said in a statement. “She has guided operations for two mayors, overseeing the city’s response to some of our most profound tragedies and crises while also guiding us through a considerable era of growth in our city that impacted operations. Metro is better for her committed diligence. Kristin has made the personal decision to resign, and I want to respect that.”

Key leaders remaining in the administration include chief of staff Masami Tyson, finance director Jenneen Reed and Choose How You Move chief program officer Sabrina Sussman. Tyler Yarbro recently succeeded Wally Dietz as legal director.  

Banner editor Steve Cavendish contributed to this story.

item.title: Aug. 18: Winter Storm Response Commission Report; DC Blox Seeks Injunction
item.dc:creator: Banner Staff
item.description:
An interim report from Mayor Freddie O'Connell's Winter Storm Response Commission recommends an evaluation of the Office of Emergency Management. DC Blox seeks a preliminary injunction against Metro's data center moratorium, and Leatrice McKissack passes away at age 96.

The post Aug. 18: Winter Storm Response Commission Report; DC Blox Seeks Injunction appeared first on Nashville Banner.
item.content:encoded:
STORM ANALYSIS: An interim report from Mayor Freddie O’Connell’s  Winter Storm Response Commission suggests that Metro perform an independent assessment of the Office of Emergency Management’s operations, organization, resources and more to ensure it meets the city’s current and future needs. Additionally, it notes a need for better communication between Nashville Electric Service and Metro entities before and during crises, better coordination with neighborhood and volunteer organizations, and more ways to reach non-English-speaking community members during a crisis. The interim report was produced after 12 public hearings, interviews with more than 60 people and an extensive review of documents from Metro offices and NES. “Our goal in creating this commission was to get an honest assessment of our whole of government and key partner performance to ensure that we will be even better positioned to serve Nashvillians when the next disaster strikes,” O’Connell said in a release. The commission’s final report is due on or before Feb. 23, 2027 and could contain additional findings and recommendations. — David Boclair

DATA DRIVEN: DC Blox has taken the next step in its legal action against Metro over its planned data center next to the Nashville Zoo, asking U.S. District Judge Eli Richardson to issue a preliminary injunction preventing Metro from enforcing its moratorium on data centers, as well as an order requiring Metro to process the company’s building, grading, zoning and development applications. The planned center has caused an uproar, and a petition from the Nashville Zoo to stop the data center has been signed by nearly 600,000 people. On Aug. 4, the Metro Council voted 27-5 to authorize Metro Legal to initiate eminent domain proceedings to take ownership of the 23.49-acre parcel on Grassmere Park Drive. “Metro’s elected officials publicly pledged to oppose, block, and delay the project,” the filing reads, “and Metro’s Director of Law told DC BLOX’s counsel that Metro would do whatever it could to prevent the project from proceeding.” The filing describes Metro’s actions as “a targeted governmental campaign directed at a particular project and property owner, not a legitimate, evenhanded exercise of Metro’s land-use authority.” — Mikeie Honda Reiland

LEATRICE McKISSACK (1930-2026): Leatrice McKissack, a groundbreaking executive and a prominent civic leader, died last week. She was 96. McKissack is an important link in the leadership of McKissack and McKissack, a minority-owned design and construction firm founded in the 1900s. A graduate of Fisk University and Tennessee State University, she taught public school for 17 years before assuming control of the company in 1983 after her husband, William McKissack, suffered a stroke. During her tenure, she and the firm earned numerous awards, including recognition from two U.S. presidents, George H.W. Bush (1990) and Bill Clinton (1994). Black Enterprise magazine named her one of America’s most successful and powerful Black businesswomen. She also created the McKissack Development Corporation to expand affordable housing opportunities in underserved communities. She is survived by three daughters and many grandchildren and great-grandchildren. — David Boclair

item.title: Metro Council Considers Limits on Drone Use by Nashville Police
item.dc:creator: Steven Hale
item.description:
The Metro Council is set to consider a bill that would restrict Nashville police from using drones except in specific emergency situations following a controversial pilot program.

The post Metro Council Considers Limits on Drone Use by Nashville Police appeared first on Nashville Banner.
item.content:encoded:
As debate about law enforcement’s embrace of surveillance technology continues to swirl around the country, the Metro Council on Tuesday will consider a bill to restrict the future use of drones by Nashville police. It comes after the Metro Nashville Police Department wrapped up its trial of a Drone as First Responder (DFR) program in Madison earlier this month. 

The proposed ordinance was originally filed last month by southeast Nashville Councilmember Sandra Sepulveda. The substitute version she’ll offer Tuesday would amend the Metro Code to explicitly require that any future DFR program be approved by the council after a public hearing. It would also limit such a program to deploying drones in response to active shooter incidents, hostage situations, active searches for missing persons, and “for a period of up to ten days, a state of emergency declared by the mayor or natural disaster that presents an immediate threat to life or critical infrastructure.” 

DFR programs are increasingly popular with police departments around the country, who present them as a way to give officers a view of crime scenes or unfolding emergencies more quickly. But the prospect of police eyes in the sky has also raised privacy concerns. 

“The normalization of police DFR programs jeopardizes privacy in communities across the country,” Beryl Lipton, senior investigative researcher for the Electronic Frontier Foundation wrote last month. “As flying cameras, drones can capture footage from areas typically inaccessible to a casual patrol officer — backyards, roofs, through windows — at distances that leave subjects of surveillance completely unaware of the spy in the sky.”

The drones used in the MNPD’s trial were provided for free by the company Skydio, but drones are also now part of the suite of surveillance products offered by companies like taser-maker Axon and leading license-plate-reader firm Flock Safety. Sepulveda told the Banner that the MNPD told councilmembers the drones were only recording video footage once they were at the scene of the incident in question.

The MNPD trial consisted of three drones based on the roof of the Madison precinct that could be used to respond to emergency calls within a two-mile radius. The MNPD has said it conducted 30 flight days between May 22 and Aug. 7. A public dashboard shows the reason, time and route for each flight. On July 29 at 2:17 p.m., a drone flew south from the precinct in response to a call regarding a vehicle wreck; on July 17 around the same time in the afternoon, one flew west toward a reported burglary at a Madison residence. 

Sepulveda told the Banner that she filed the bill in large part because of frustration with the MNPD launching a trial drone program without including the public or most of the council. The Banner first reported in April that the department was planning such a trial after receiving a waiver from the Federal Aviation Administration permitting it to conduct operations using drones that are out of an officer’s line of sight. The department has argued that its DFR trial was exempt from an existing Metro ordinance requiring council approval for surveillance technology because the drones were provided at no cost and without a contract. 

“Regardless of how many of us councilmembers feel — many are in support, there are many who are against — the public didn’t get any input,” Sepulveda said. 

She added that she doesn’t see any reason for the use of drones in many cases. While the uses her bill would allow — like an active shooter — are closer to the type cited by DFR boosters, data from the MNPD trial shows drones were launched in response to a far wider spectrum of incidents. They include reports of a person with a weapon and an explosion along with calls for a “suspicious” and “disorderly” people. Reports from community advocates and Nashville’s Community Review Board have highlighted the fact that drone flights during the trial program were conducted in disproportionately Black and brown communities and low-income areas. 

An MNPD presentation on its trial program on Aug. 7 was announced and then abruptly closed to the public. 

The original, more broadly written version of Sepulveda’s bill prompted Metro Police Chief John Drake to write a letter urging councilmembers to oppose it. He wrote that the legislation “threatens the safety of officers and the public,” adding a long list of scenarios for which he feared drone use would be banned. 

“The public safety value of this tool cannot be overstated,” Drake wrote in the message sent to the council on July 31. “The failure to utilize drones in situations where it could save officer and citizen lives would be negligent at best, reckless at worst.”

He also wrote that the bill would affect the ability of Metro’s Office of Emergency Management and the Nashville Fire Department to deploy drones during “lifesaving operations.” 

Sepulveda told the Banner that she worked on the new version of her bill with community advocates and the mayor’s office and ensured that it would not hinder the use of drones by other departments. 

“This is specifically targeted to the drones as first responders,” she said. 

Her bill also prohibits the use of facial recognition technology and autonomous drones.

The post Metro Council Considers Limits on Drone Use by Nashville Police appeared first on Nashville Banner.

item.title: Nashville Metro Council Advances Drone Restrictions, Music City Funding Bills
item.dc:creator: Stephen Elliott
item.description:
The Metro Council advanced legislation to refinance Music City Center debt and transfer $300 million to East Bank infrastructure, while also moving forward with a bill regarding MNPD drone surveillance restrictions.

The post Nashville Metro Council Advances Drone Restrictions, Music City Funding Bills appeared first on Nashville Banner.
item.content:encoded:
Two pieces of legislation that would allow refinancing of Music City Center debt and the transfer of $300 million in excess tourism tax revenues to be spent on East Bank infrastructure advanced at Tuesday’s Metro Council meeting. 

The resolution passed 31-6, while the bill passed its second reading and will be back for a final vote on Sept. 1. 

Councilmembers Sean Parker and Quin Evans Segall raised questions about the proposal during a meeting of the council’s East Bank committee late last month. Debate continued at Monday’s meeting of the East Bank committee, which recommended passage of the bills on 4-3 votes. The legislation includes the extension of certain tax revenue streams that are currently dedicated to the Music City Center. 

“I’m afraid that we are doubling down on the mistakes of the past here,” Parker said during the full council meeting, referencing the original Music City Center financing structure that collected significantly more money than necessary to pay for the project. 

Metro Finance Director Jenneen Reed addressed the questions during a Budget Committee meeting earlier this month. She presented an estimate that the tax dollars Metro could recapture by eliminating the revenue streams would be less than the financial benefit of passing the legislation. 

The $300 million transfer will go toward East Bank projects, some of which Metro would have to pay for on its own. Refinancing the Music City Center debt would also release Metro’s “backstop” of that debt, Reed said, freeing up capacity for the city to stand up an affordable housing bond program. 

The legislation also allows the Music City Center to fund an expansion that could cost up to $1 billion. The proposal was initiated by the Tennessee General Assembly earlier this year, with House Speaker Cameron Sexton, who sits on the East Bank Development Authority, seeking a funding stream for that body. Other elements of the legislation include annual payments to Metro for public safety and, if enough excess revenue comes in, support for major events downtown and grants to businesses downtown, with the grants controlled by a new state board. 

Evans Segall said residents would be “appalled” by the grants to downtown businesses but not other businesses or residents. 

Councilmember Delishia Porterfield said, “there are things about this I like, things about this I don’t like.”

She ultimately was among those voting for the legislation, noting that Metro did not have the authority to redirect the revenue streams established by the state. 

Metro Legal is currently reviewing new emergency rules issued by the Tennessee Department of Tourist Development in response to recent state legislation about tourism development zones like the one encompassing Nashville’s Lower Broad area. The rules restrict the local government’s ability to close streets and institute restrictions on loitering. 

Drones

A bill that passed its second of three readings would restrict the use of drones for surveillance. The legislation, helmed by lead sponsor Councilmember Sandra Sepulveda, follows the recent conclusion of the Metro Nashville Police Department’s test of a drone program. The bill passed on a voice vote with two members voting no. Third and final reading will follow at the Sept. 1 meeting. 

MNPD Deputy Chief Chris Gilder told councilmembers during Tuesday’s Public Health and Safety Committee that the department appreciated the changes made in the substitute that advanced. He also said that the department would prefer to be able to use the technology for more uses than those listed in the legislation. 

Benjamin Davis, a resident who supports the drone restrictions, said during public comment that “the people of Nashville are sick of being recorded without their consent.”

Council leadership 

Councilmembers Olivia Hill and Jeff Preptit were nominated by colleagues to serve as the body’s president pro tempore, the leadership position that runs the council in the absence of the vice mayor and oversees pre-meeting announcement periods. Porterfield is wrapping up her one-year term in the role, and whoever is elected at the Sept. 1 meeting will serve out the final year of this council’s time in office. 

The council could have another type of leader soon. Metro opened the job posting for Metro Council special counsel and legislative services division director on Tuesday. The senior staff role is responsible for legal review of legislation, drafting bills and other legal advice. The leader of the Metro Council office previously served as both special counsel and council office director. Since Margaret Darby left the position at the end of 2025, Brian Wilson has been serving in an interim capacity. The body has split the role into two positions, a special counsel and a chief of staff. 

Tuesday marked the final meeting for committee chairs, as Vice Mayor Angie Henderson announced appointments for the final year of the term last week. See the list at the bottom of this story. 

The rest

  • Councilmember Joy Styles is back with another push to require Metro departments, boards and commissions to conduct annual employee surveys. The bill passed its first of three readings. She withdrew a similar effort earlier this year. It was inspired by problems at the Department of Emergency Communications, whose director was ultimately fired. 
  • An amendment to the previously approved plan for a major development along Gallatin Avenue in East Nashville passed its final vote. Some neighbors have objected to changes to the development of the former auto-diesel college campus. Councilmember Sean Parker added an amendment that adds conditions about open space and traffic signals, and caps the number of single-family detached homes in the project. 
  • Councilmember Jennifer Frensley Webb’s legislation adding contextual overlays in an area around Gallatin Pike in Madison passed their third and final votes. They were both unanimously disapproved by the Metro Planning Commission, meaning they faced a higher vote threshold. That disapproval also triggered some contention at the Aug. 4 Metro Council meeting, when Webb criticized the commission and its Metro Council representative, Rollin Horton. “This shouldn’t be controversial,” Webb said Tuesday, stating that the overlays were desired by her constituents and wouldn’t directly limit density in the area.

The post Nashville Metro Council Advances Drone Restrictions, Music City Funding Bills appeared first on Nashville Banner.

item.title: Nashville Sues Trump Administration Over Attempt to Withhold First-Responder Grants to Force Election Changes
item.dc:creator: Steve Cavendish
item.description:
Nashville joined several other jurisdictions in a federal lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security, alleging that withholding grant funding to enforce new election administration requirements violates constitutional authority.

The post Nashville Sues Trump Administration Over Attempt to Withhold First-Responder Grants to Force Election Changes appeared first on Nashville Banner.
item.content:encoded:
Nashville filed suit against the federal government for attempting to make changes to how local elections are administered as a condition Department of Homeland Security grants that the city uses for first responders.

The lawsuit, which was filed in federal court in the D.C. Circuit Monday morning, alleges the grant system, administered by FEMA, is a violation of separation of powers as well as the authority of states to administer elections enshrined in the Constitution.

“FEMA has no authority to impose those conditions — not under its governing statute and not under the Constitution,” the suit argues. “Congress authorized FEMA to help jurisdictions protect critical infrastructure from terrorist and cyberattacks. It did not authorize FEMA to decide who may vote, how ballots must be counted, or how states maintain their voter rolls. Never before has FEMA purported to regulate how states and counties run elections. Such a transformative assertion of federal authority in an area of traditional state control requires clear congressional authorization that FEMA does not have. The power to administer elections belongs to the states, subject only to conditions imposed by Congress — not the President, not the Secretary of Homeland Security, and not FEMA.”

Metro joined three other jurisdictions in the suit: Columbus, Ohio; Harris County, Texas; and El Paso County, Texas. 

Failure to implement these changes would result in a 20 percent cut of the DHS grant to Metro, which the city has used for rapid response capabilities. In the last three years, grants totaling approximately $3 million were used to acquire handheld spectrometers to assess hazardous radioactive and biological threats, train personnel on situations involving structural collapse and purchase equipment and training related to chemical threats.

Further failure to comply could ultimately result in losing the entire grant.

“This lawsuit seeks to secure necessary funding that would provide equipment and training to Nashville’s first responders in handling emergency or terrorist events in our city,” Metro Director of Law Tyler Yarbro said. “The Trump administration wants to withhold those funds unless we implement wholly unnecessary and costly changes to our election procedures. Courts have consistently rejected the administration’s efforts to meddle in elections. We are proud to join other cities and counties across the country to ensure that our access to federal funds designated for first responders is protected.”

The policy, which was announced a month ago, targets states and “high-risk urban election jurisdictions” with five conditions. Jurisdictions must:

  • Transition to hand-marked paper ballots
  • Conduct a manual audit of at least five percent of the votes cast in a federal election
  • Reconcile the number of voters with the number of ballots cast
  • Verify voter citizenship through the federal Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system 
  • Use the SAVE system to verify poll workers

The Davidson County Election Commission has used a combination of ballot marking devices with touch screens since 2006. The suit states that the entire setup would have to be changed to accommodate hand-marked ballots, incurring equipment costs and retraining of the staff and reeducation of the county’s electorate.

The suit comes after an audit of the Aug. 6 primary by the Davidson County Election Commission last week found zero errors in the count and no problem in the administration of the primary. 

The suit is the first major action by Metro Legal since Yarbro succeeded Wally Dietz as the director of law. Dietz led a robust response to the Trump Administration’s campaign of executive orders over the last two years, joining with the Public Rights Project to sign onto suits to fight cancellation of transit, public health and anti-homelessness funding.

“DHS is trying to use homeland security funding to dramatically reshape how local governments run their elections,” said Toby Merrill, litigation director for Public Rights Project. “These new conditions would undermine the local control that has helped make our elections safe and secure for decades. We’re proud to stand with cities and counties fighting to protect their communities from this harmful federal overreach.”

The post Nashville Sues Trump Administration Over Attempt to Withhold First-Responder Grants to Force Election Changes appeared first on Nashville Banner.
